sources.author: MIT OpenCourseWare
sources.excerpt: Algorithm analysis connects a precise problem specification to a correctness argument and resource bounds. Asymptotic notation describes how resource use grows with input size. A loop invariant supports a proof by initialization, maintenance, and termination. Divide-and-conquer algorithms split a problem, solve subproblems, and combine their results. Recurrences describe the cost of recursive algorithms. Graph algorithms operate on vertices and edges to answer reachability, ordering, connectivity, and path questions. Dynamic programming records solutions to overlapping subproblems. Core methods include sorting, hashing, trees, graphs, shortest paths, and dynamic programming. A disciplined solution states inputs and outputs, proves correctness, and then analyzes time and space.
sources.title: MIT OpenCourseWare Introduction to Algorithms

sources.author: OpenDSA Project
sources.excerpt: OpenDSA presents data structures and algorithms through executable visualizations and exercises. Lists represent ordered sequences with position-based operations. Stacks use last-in, first-out access, while queues use first-in, first-out access. Trees represent hierarchical relationships and support recursive traversals. Hash tables map keys to locations and require a collision strategy. Graphs can be represented with adjacency structures for traversal and path algorithms. Automata and formal languages describe machines, accepted strings, and computational limits. Representation choices and invariants determine which operations are efficient and which errors are possible.
